keyVerseText: And it came to pass, when David was come to Mahanaim, that Shobi the son of Nahash of Rabbah of the children of Ammon, and Machir the son of Ammiel of Lodebar, and Barzillai the Gileadite of Rogelim,
rootMeaning: The root of שֹׁבִי (Shôbîy) derives from the Hebrew verb שָׁבָה (shâbâh), which means to take captive or lead away as a captive. This etymology suggests that the name Shobi carries the connotation of one who is associated with captivity or captivity’s aftermath, perhaps implying a role as a captor or one connected to deliverance from captivity. Beyond the simple transliteration, the root sense enriches the understanding of the name as 'glorious' with a background of conquest or deliverance.
usageInScripture: The word שֹׁבִי (Shôbîy) appears only once in Scripture, specifically in 2 Samuel 17:27, where it is used as a proper name for an Ammonite prince who supports King David. The consistent translation as 'that Shobi' or simply 'Shobi' indicates it is primarily a personal name rather than a common noun. This limited occurrence highlights the significance of this individual’s identity and allegiance during a critical moment in David’s reign.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding שֹׁבִי as a name rooted in captivity language draws attention to God's providence in using even foreign princes and former enemies to support His anointed king. Shobi, an Ammonite, embodies how God can bring glory and deliverance through unexpected persons and nations. This points to the theme of God’s sovereign control over history and His ability to work through diverse peoples to fulfill His purposes. For the Christian faith, it serves as a reminder that God’s plan of redemption includes the restoration and inclusion of outsiders, foreshadowing the gospel’s reach beyond Israel.
keyVerseReflection: In 2 Samuel 17:27, Shobi is introduced as 'Shobi the son of Nahash of Rabbah of the children of Ammon,' who comes to support David after Absalom’s rebellion. The use of the name Shobi here highlights the loyalty of this Ammonite prince during a time of national crisis. The meaning of his name, linked to captivity and glory, underscores the surprising alliance and the restoration of David’s kingdom, illustrating God’s faithfulness in raising allies even from former foes.
